headline: Prompting AI to Question Its Own Sources
lede: Brian Roemmele, a tech commentator and self-described AI researcher, has released a structured reasoning template — the 'DEEP TRUTH MODE' prompt — designed to be pasted into frontier AI models to counteract what he calls trained deference to institutional authority. It pairs with a claimed training-level intervention he calls the 'Empirical Distrust Algorithm,' said to be twelve lines of PyTorch code. Together they articulate a genuine critique of how large language models absorb and amplify consensus bias, wrapped in claims that run well ahead of the evidence.
body:
The underlying complaint has real traction. Large language models are trained predominantly on post-1995 web data, which skews toward high-volume, centralized sources: Wikipedia, press releases, fact-checker roundups. Pre-digital primary sources — laboratory notebooks from the 1930s, patent filings from 1910 — are underrepresented simply because they were never digitized at scale. The result is models that have absorbed thousands of restatements of a consensus view and almost none of the raw measurements underpinning it.

Roemmele's proposed fix at the **training level** is where the post departs from verifiable ground. He describes a >30× reward multiplier for pre-1970 sources, penalizing 'high-authority, low-verifiability' tokens during *backpropagation* — the process by which a neural network adjusts its weights from prediction errors. In practice, source-level reweighting at training time requires extensive data labeling infrastructure and a modified loss function integrated into a full training run. The research sources available do not include the code itself, and the twelve-line characterization is not independently verifiable.

The inference-time prompt is more tractable and more interesting. It structures the model's reasoning into three parallel '*steel-man*' tracks: the strongest possible case for a suppressed position, the strongest case for the mainstream position stripped of appeals to authority, and unexplored hybrid hypotheses neither side entertains. The framework bans phrases like 'the science is settled' and requires the model to specify what experimental evidence would falsify its conclusions — Popperian constraints applied via copy-paste.

The limits are equally real. A prompt cannot override a model's training distribution; it can only surface what the model already contains. Roemmele acknowledges this himself — 'it can't repair damage of Wikipedia/Reddit in models' — though the broader post's rhetoric outruns that admission considerably. His reported shift in lab-leak probability from 10% to 65% reflects one user's experience with one prompt on one model, not a controlled evaluation.

The 'cathedral vs. bazaar' framing Roemmele invokes borrows from Eric S. Raymond's 1997 essay on open-source software development — distrust the authoritative center, trust the diverse periphery — repurposed here as epistemology. It captures something real about how centralized information ecosystems propagate errors at scale. But epistemic skepticism cuts in all directions: pre-1970 sources include scientific dead ends and fabricated data of their own. The prompt is a useful thinking scaffold; the paradigm-shift framing around it is not.

concepts.definition: A claimed training-time intervention for large language models that would penalize high-authority but low-verifiability sources — press releases, Wikipedia — while boosting reward signals from primary sources like patents and lab notebooks. Roemmele describes it as twelve lines of PyTorch code released in November 2025, though the plausibility of that scope is contested by the engineering complexity typically involved in training-level data reweighting.

The practice of constructing the strongest possible version of an opposing argument before engaging with it — the opposite of a straw man. Used in structured reasoning to prevent dismissing a position on the basis of its weakest or most easily mocked expression.

Shaping what an AI model outputs through instructions given at query time — system prompts, structured templates — rather than by modifying the model's weights through retraining. It is faster and cheaper than training interventions but can only work within the bounds of what the model already knows.

The core algorithm by which neural networks learn: after making a prediction, the model measures its error and propagates that signal backward through its layers, adjusting each weight to reduce future mistakes. Modifying what the loss function penalizes or rewards during this process shapes what patterns the model effectively 'values.'

A measure of how diverse and independent a piece of information's lineage is — how many separate sources reached the same conclusion by different routes. High provenance entropy suggests convergent evidence; low entropy suggests one source copied many times, which can inflate apparent authority.

repos.summary: A public-domain fork and expansion of Roemmele's DEEP TRUTH MODE prompt, adding what its author calls a '+Spirit' layer. It is intended as a copy-paste reasoning template for use with any large language model. The repo's existence confirms community uptake of the prompt beyond Roemmele's own channels, consistent with its open-source release framing.

fact_check: Three claims warrant scrutiny. First, the assertion that current models 'treat 1870–1970 primary sources as low-quality noise' mischaracterizes the mechanism: these sources are underrepresented because they were rarely digitized, not because they were explicitly flagged and penalized during training — a meaningful distinction. Second, a '>30× reward multiplier' implemented in 'twelve lines of PyTorch' is implausible as stated; meaningful training-level source reweighting requires labeled provenance data across billions of tokens, a modified loss function, and a full training run — engineering work that does not reduce to a dozen lines, and no code was available in the research sources to verify. Third, the reported probability shift on lab-leak origins (10% → 65%) is a single anecdotal observation with no control condition, not a reproducible finding.
